beef-rice-and-vegetables-excluding-carro.title: Beef, rice, and vegetables without carrots, broccoli, and dark-green leafy; gravy

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of lean beef, boiled rice, and a selection of vegetables, excluding carrots, broccoli, and dark‑green leafy greens. It is served with a flavorful gravy that adds richness to the meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef is an excellent source of complete protein and iron.
Rice provides complex carbohydrates that give sustained energy.
Excluding carrots, broccoli, and leafy greens is often done due to allergies or specific dietary restrictions.
Gravy can be made from broth, tomato base, or cream, altering its taste profile.
Traditionally the dish is served hot, often accompanied by a side of permitted vegetables.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef supplies all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Energy provision
items.content: Rice delivers glucose that is quickly converted into usable energy.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Beef contains iron, zinc, and vitamin B12, supporting blood formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Low fiber content
items.content: The omission of carrots, broccoli, and leafy greens reduces dietary fiber, which can be beneficial for certain gastrointestinal conditions.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both beef and rice are rich in B1, B3, and B6 vitamins, aiding metabolic processes.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Even lean beef contains saturated fats; individuals with high cholesterol should monitor portion size.

items.title: Sodium in gravy
items.content: Prepared gravies can be high in salt; low‑sodium versions or homemade sauces are recommended.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Rare but possible allergic reactions to beef may occur.

items.title: Lack of fiber
items.content: Excluding fiber‑rich vegetables may diminish the digestive benefits of the meal.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, combining beef, rice, and the allowed vegetables. Drizzle the gravy over the top or serve it on the side. Fresh herbs such as parsley or dill can be added for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. If frozen, it lasts up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C.

chicken-drumstick-baked-or-broiled-skin-.title: Chicken drumstick, baked or broiled, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken drumsticks are the lower leg portion of the bird, containing meat, skin, and a small amount of bone. When baked or broiled, they stay juicy and flavorful. The skin is edible and adds a crisp texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken drumsticks are a staple in many traditional dishes worldwide.
Baking or broiling makes the skin crispy while keeping the meat tender.
Chicken is one of the most affordable sources of high‑quality protein.
In some cuisines the drumsticks are served with barbecue or honey‑mustard sauces.
Pre‑cooked drumsticks can be frozen for quick meals later.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken drumsticks provide complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system health.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from chicken helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Provides zinc
items.content: Zinc is important for immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Drumsticks fit well into low‑carb and ketogenic eating plans.

items.title: Food allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared marinades or sauces can add significant sodium.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking may allow salmonella growth.

items.title: Skin fat
items.content: The skin contains saturated fat; those monitoring cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken drumsticks can be served as a main dish, sliced into salads, used in sandwiches, or added to soups. The skin can be eaten crispy or removed for a leaner option.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh drumsticks in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen drumsticks store at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw in the fridge before cooking, not at room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Frozen daiquiri is a refreshing cocktail made with rum, lime juice, and sugar, served in a frozen slush form. It blends the tartness of lime with sweet smoothness, creating a light, aromatic drink popular in warm weather.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The original daiquiri was created in the early 20th century in Cuba as a simple mix of rum, lime, and sugar.
The frozen version appeared in the United States in the 1970s thanks to the rise of blenders.
White rum is commonly used, but flavored rums can add interesting twists.
There are many variations, including berry, tropical fruit, and spice-infused versions.
Some restaurants serve frozen daiquiri topped with whipped cream and grated chocolate.

items.title: Vitamin C from lime
items.content: Lime provides vitamin C, supporting the immune system and acting as an antioxidant.

items.title: Beneficial polyphenols from rum
items.content: In moderate amounts, rum contains polyphenols that may help protect cardiovascular health.

items.title: Hydration in heat
items.content: A frozen drink helps maintain fluid balance during hot weather.

items.title: Alcohol content
items.content: The alcohol makes the drink unsuitable for children, pregnant women, and individuals with contraindications.

items.title: Sugar load
items.content: High sugar levels can raise blood glucose, so people with diabetes should limit portions.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Lime may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve frozen daiquiri in tall glasses, garnish with a lime wedge, mint, or fresh berries. Adding fruit chunks to the blender creates a more vibrant flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The cocktail is best enjoyed immediately. If you need to store it, keep it in an airtight container in the freezer for no more than 24 hours to prevent excessive crystallization.

mustard-greens-frozen-cooked-fat-added.title: Mustard greens, frozen, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Mustard greens (Brassica juncea) are a leafy vegetable rich in vitamins and minerals. In the frozen form the leaves are blanched, then a small amount of fat is added to improve flavor and texture. The product is ready to eat after reheating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mustard greens belong to the cruciferous family, along with broccoli and cabbage.
The raw leaves have a peppery bite that mellows with heat.
Freezing preserves most of the vitamins, especially vitamin C and carotenoids.
In Asian cuisines mustard greens are common in salads, soups, and stir‑fries.
Adding a little oil enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: Support vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: An antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Provides folate
items.content: Important for DNA synthesis and cell division, especially during pregnancy.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Cruciferous allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to mustard greens.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: High oxalate levels can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

items.title: Added fat
items.content: The product contains added fat, so those monitoring calorie intake should account for it.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reheat mustard greens in the microwave or a skillet, add them to soups, stews, pasta dishes, or use as a filling for wraps. They pair well with rice, quinoa, and legumes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen product in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once thawed, consume within 2–3 days and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator.

content.title: About
content.content: Peanut butter with reduced sodium and sugar is made from roasted peanuts with less added salt and sugar. It retains the classic nutty flavor while being less salty and sweet, making it suitable for low‑sodium and low‑sugar diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanut butter is a popular alternative to butter and is widely used in sports nutrition.
Reduced salt and sugar make it a better choice for people with hypertension or diabetes risk.
It is rich in monounsaturated fats, which are considered heart‑healthy.
Unlike many nut spreads, peanut butter can stay creamy without added emulsifiers.
Peanuts are legumes, not true nuts, which matters for certain nut allergy considerations.

items.title: Rich in healthy fats
items.content: The majority of fats are monounsaturated, supporting cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Approximately 25 % of the product’s weight is protein, aiding muscle repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as a powerful antioxidant protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: Reduced salt helps maintain healthy blood pressure levels.

items.title: Reduced sugar
items.content: Less added sugar lowers the product’s glycemic impact.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanut butter can trigger severe allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Despite lower sodium and sugar, it remains calorie‑dense, so portion control is important.

items.title: Aflatoxin risk
items.content: Improperly processed peanuts may contain aflatoxins; choose products from reputable manufacturers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread on toast, stir into smoothies, yogurt, oatmeal, or use in sauces and baked goods. For lower calorie intake, use modest portions.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. For extended shelf life, store in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Pepperoni pizza is a popular school lunch option. A medium crust provides a crunchy base, while slices of spicy pepperoni add flavor and a hint of heat. The pizza is served hot, often with tomato sauce and a modest amount of cheese.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pepperoni is an American version of Italian salami, made from pork and beef.
A medium crust is considered ideal for balancing crispness and softness.
Pizza is frequently included in school menus as a quick source of carbs and protein.
Tomato sauce in pizza is rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that retains its bright red color when baked.
Some schools bake pizza in specialized ovens that reach the required temperature quickly.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Pepperoni and cheese provide a substantial amount of protein needed for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Carbohydrates from the crust give a rapid source of energy, important for active students.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough and meat ingredients contain vitamins B1, B2 and B6, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Lycopene has antioxidant properties and may help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds calcium, essential for bone and tooth development in children.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Salt in the sauce and pepperoni can lead to exceeding the daily recommended sodium intake.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Meat toppings and cheese contain saturated fats, which should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in children with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate
items.content: Some sauces may contain added MSG, which can cause headaches in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pepperoni pizza is typically eaten hot, cut into serving slices. Adding fresh vegetables such as tomatoes or arugula can balance flavor and boost nutrient content.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftover pizza in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or microwave to restore crust crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Queso Anejo is an aged Mexican cheese made from cow’s milk, maturing for 3 to 12 months. During aging it develops a firm, crystalline texture, bright orange hue, and a strong nutty‑caramel flavor with a hint of sharpness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “anejo” means “old” in Spanish, highlighting its long aging period.
Traditionally produced in the Mexican states of Oaxaca and Chiapas, where the climate favors slow maturation.
Tyrosine crystals form during aging, giving the cheese its characteristic crunchy “grainy” sensation.
Often grated over tacos, enchiladas, and guacamole to add depth of flavor.
When tightly wrapped, the cheese can be stored for up to a year in the refrigerator.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Queso Anejo contains more calcium than most soft cheeses, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: A serving provides about 20 g of high‑quality protein, aiding muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The cheese supplies vitamin B12, riboflavin, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Probiotic properties
items.content: Fermentation promotes beneficial bacteria that may help maintain a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low lactose content
items.content: Extended aging breaks down most lactose, making the cheese more tolerable for people with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to casein or whey may experience reactions ranging from mild to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: The cheese is salty; those with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of its high fat content, Queso Anejo is calorie‑dense; moderation is key for weight management.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: A large proportion of the fat is saturated, so people with elevated cholesterol should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Grate Queso Anejo over tortillas, add it to soups, salads, and casseroles, or serve small chunks as a snack with fruit or nuts. For maximum aroma, grate the cheese using a coarse grater just before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cheese in an airtight container or wrapped in wax paper in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. For longer storage (over 3 months) it can be frozen, though the texture will become more crumbly.

content.title: About
content.content: Split pea soup is made from yellow or green dried peas, water, vegetables, and seasonings. It has a thick, creamy texture and a hearty aroma typical of traditional Northern European and American cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The soup is often served with smoked ham or bacon to deepen the flavor.
Traditional split pea soup is a national dish of the Netherlands (Erwtensoep) and the United States (Pea Soup).
Dried peas are split in half, which speeds up cooking and creates a smoother consistency.
It is commonly prepared in large batches and frozen – the taste improves after reheating.
Some recipes add carrots, leeks, and celery for extra brightness.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peas provide about 8 g of protein per 100 g of dry product, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Peas contain thiamine, folate, and vitamin B6, important for metabolism.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Peas supply iron, magnesium, phosphorus, and zinc, supporting blood health and nerve function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Split pea soup contains virtually no saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Legumes can cause increased gas in sensitive people.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Peas contain purines, so people with gout should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot, often with a slice of rye bread or croutons. It can be made ahead, stored in the refrigerator for up to 3 days, or frozen for up to 3 months.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dried peas in a cool, dry place in an airtight container. Store prepared soup in a sealed container in the fridge, and freeze in portion‑size containers for longer storage.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet potato tots are small, deep‑fried or baked balls made from grated sweet potato, often seasoned and coated with breadcrumbs. They have a crispy exterior and a soft, slightly sweet interior characteristic of sweet potatoes. Tots are popular as a snack or side in fast‑food restaurants, quick‑serve eateries, and street‑food stalls.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet potatoes are richer in beta‑carotene than regular potatoes, giving the tots a bright orange hue.
Sweet potato tots gained popularity in the United States in the early 2000s as a healthier alternative to traditional potato croquettes.
Some recipes add corn starch to the mixture to create an extra‑crunchy crust.
Tots are often served with yogurt‑based dips, salsa, or honey‑mustard sauces.
Sweet potatoes are grown in tropical and subtropical regions, but are available year‑round in many countries.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene converts to vitamin A in the body, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Lower glycemic index than regular potatoes
items.content: Sweet potato tots cause a slower rise in blood sugar compared with regular potato fries.

items.title: Source of potassium and vitamin C
items.content: These nutrients help maintain heart health and antioxidant defenses.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Antioxidants help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Sweet potato allergy
items.content: Although rare, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to sweet potatoes.

items.title: High calorie content when fried
items.content: Because tots are often deep‑fried, they can be calorie‑dense; moderation is advised.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Added salt or sauces can increase sodium intake, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve sweet potato tots hot as a snack, side dish for burgers, or in a lunch box. Dip them in yogurt, garlic aioli, honey‑mustard, or spicy chili sauce. For a lighter option, bake them in the oven instead of frying.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked tots in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Uncooked, frozen tots keep for up to 2 months; thaw and fry or bake before serving.

tea-iced-brewed-black-decaffeinated-pre-.title: Tea, iced, brewed, black, decaffeinated, pre-sweetened with sugar

content.title: About
content.content: This product is a ready‑to‑drink iced tea made from black tea that has been decaffeinated and sweetened with sugar. It comes in convenient packaging and requires no further preparation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black tea is rich in polyphenols, which have antioxidant properties.
Decaffeination preserves most flavor notes while removing almost all caffeine.
Sweetening with sugar makes the beverage sweeter and raises its calorie count.
Iced tea is a popular refreshing drink during the summer months.
Cold‑brew technology can reduce the bitterness typical of hot‑brewed tea.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Black tea provides flavonoids that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The drink contributes to maintaining the body’s fluid balance, especially in warm weather.

items.title: Stress reduction
items.content: Theanine present in tea may promote relaxation without causing drowsiness.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Both warm and cold teas can aid normal gastrointestinal function.

items.title: Energy support
items.content: Although caffeine is removed, other bioactive compounds can give a mild boost in alertness.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Added sugar can raise blood glucose levels and increase the beverage’s caloric load.

items.title: Tea allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to tea components.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Tea may increase stomach acidity, which can be problematic for people with gastritis or reflux.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink the iced tea straight from the package or pour it over ice in a glass. For extra flavor, add a slice of lemon or a sprig of mint.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑sodium teriyaki sauce is a flavorful Asian condiment made from soy sauce, sugar, vinegar, ginger, and garlic, but with less salt (≈ 0.5 g per 100 ml). It gives dishes a sweet‑salty taste without overwhelming them with sodium.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Teriyaki means “sweet‑salty” in Japanese.
The lower sodium level is achieved by replacing part of the salt with potassium chloride or using naturally low‑salt fermented soybeans.
Teriyaki sauce is commonly used as a glaze or marinade for meat, fish, tofu, and vegetables.
Sugar in the sauce can be swapped for honey, maple syrup, or stevia for a healthier version.
Homemade teriyaki allows precise control over salt and sugar content.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Soy sauce, the base ingredient, provides plant‑based protein that supports tissue repair.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Ginger and garlic are rich in antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Ginger stimulates gastric secretions, aiding digestion.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: Reduced salt makes the sauce more suitable for people monitoring blood pressure.

items.title: Flavorful with fewer calories
items.content: The sweet‑salty profile lets you use less sauce, saving calories.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to soy should avoid this sauce.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Despite lower sodium, the sauce may still contain notable sugar, important for diabetics.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate (MSG)
items.content: Some commercial versions add MSG, which can cause sensitivity in certain people.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Sugar and oil add calories; moderate consumption is advised.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Use the sauce as a marinade for meat, fish, or tofu, as a glaze when grilling, pan‑frying, or baking, and stir it into rice, noodle dishes, or salads. It also works well as a dip for vegetables and sushi rolls.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Refrigerate after opening in a tightly sealed bottle. Keep for up to 3 months. Discard if color, smell, or taste changes.
